title: Shiloh
lead: A town in the hills of Ephraim where Israel set up the tent of meeting after the conquest and kept the ark until the Philistine wars. Its ruin became a warning that God's house can be lost (Joshua 18:1; 1 Samuel 1–4; Psalm 78:60; Jeremiah 7:12–14). Not to be confused with the debated "Shiloh" of Genesis 49:10 (see the topic on the Messiah).

sections.b: Judges 21:19 places Shiloh "north of Bethel, east of the road from Bethel to Shechem," which fits Khirbet Seilun. The tribes gather there to divide the land (Joshua 18–22), and the town keeps a yearly feast with dancing girls (Judges 21:19–21). Hannah prays there, and the boy Samuel serves under Eli (1 Samuel 1–3). After the ark is taken in battle (1 Samuel 4), Shiloh drops out of the story. Psalm 78:60 says God "left the tabernacle of Shiloh behind," and Jeremiah 7:12–14 and 26:6–9 warn that Jerusalem's temple could go the same way. The prophet Ahijah still lived there in Jeroboam's time (1 Kings 14:2).

sections.b: Three campaigns have dug at Khirbet Seilun. A Danish expedition led by Hans Kjær worked there in 1926–32, and its finds were published by Marie-Louise Buhl and Svend Holm-Nielsen in 1969. Israel Finkelstein excavated in 1981–84 and found a town of the early Iron Age, which he dated as destroyed around 1050 BC. Many link that destruction with the Philistine victory of 1 Samuel 4 and the ruin remembered in Jeremiah 7:12–14, though this is an interpretation and the dating is debated. Excavations led by Scott Stripling since 2017 have made further claims, among them about where the tabernacle stood, which other archaeologists contest.
